 1 Task Description
 DOLFYN has been developed by Henk Krüs from Cyclone Fluid Dynamics BV and is available as open-source-software (www.dolfyn.net). It is a program for the analysis of complex flow phenomena:
 • Fluid mechanic (Navier-Stokes equations)
 • Turbulence models for high Reynold numbers
 • Free Surfaces for Fluids
 • Heat Conduction and Convection
 The program is a general unstructured 3D Finite Volume solver. Although it is possible to use volumes of any shape, for Post and Preprocessing it is more common to have only tetrahedra, Hexahedra or wedges with a triangular base area. This allows an easy connection to other Finite Element codes.

The program is a general unstructured 3D Finite Volume solver. Although it is possible to use volumes of any shape, for Post and Preprocessing it is more common to have only tetrahedra, Hexahedra or wedges with a triangular base area. This allows an easy connection to other Finite Element codes..
 However, SOFiSTiK provides also higher polyhedra cell types of the so called "dual mesh". The solution is then obtained for the nodes of the primary mesh, which has strong advantages for computing time and precision in 3D.
 DOLFYN has been adopted to the SOFiSTiK-environment by importing the mesh, material and boundary conditions from the data base and saving results for postprocessing into the data base. All Pre- and Postprocessing tools of SOFiSTiK may be used therefore.

It shows, from left to right, a sequence of coherent vortical structures (often called Kelvin–Helmholtz billows) developing along what appears to be the interface between two fluid streams. On the far left, the shear layer is just beginning to roll up, and the perturbations are small and barely distinguishable from the ambient fluid. As one follows the flow downstream (to the right), the instabilities grow in amplitude and roll up into discrete, mushroom-shaped vortices. These vortices then pair and merge, forming larger, more irregular swirling regions toward the right side of the frame.

The background behind the vortices is a uniform, light gray tone, providing contrast so that the darker, textured eddies stand out sharply. The individual eddies exhibit a mix of smooth curvature (at their outer rims) and more chaotic, filamentary substructures in their cores—typical of a transition from organized roll-ups to fully developed two-dimensional turbulence.

The image is a clean, black-and-white line drawing labeled “Figure 2.2: Boundary layers.” It is divided into two side-by-side panels, each depicting how a fluid’s velocity profile develops above a flat, horizontal wall (represented by a thick black bar at the bottom of each panel). Both panels share the same coordinate reference: a vertical axis labeled “z” (with an arrowhead pointing upward) anchored at the wall surface.

Left Panel – Velocity‐Profile Shapes
• Wall: a heavy horizontal line at the bottom, indicating the solid boundary where the fluid velocity is zero.  
• Vertical Axis: a thin line rising from the wall’s left end, labeled “z →,” denoting distance normal to the wall.  
• Laminar Curve: drawn closest to the wall as a smooth, gently convex curve that starts at zero velocity, then gradually bends upward and toward the right. The label “laminar” sits above this curve.  
• Turbulent Curve: plotted to the right of the laminar one, this profile rises more steeply near the wall—indicating a higher local velocity gradient—then flattens out sooner as it approaches the free‐stream region. The word “turbulent” is placed alongside this thicker, fuller curve.  
• Interpretation: the two curves illustrate that in laminar flow the velocity increases more gradually through the boundary layer, whereas in turbulent flow the near‐wall shear (and hence initial velocity rise) is higher, producing a fuller profile that reaches the free‐stream level over a somewhat thicker layer.

Right Panel – Schematic Boundary‐Layer Thickness
• Wall and z‐Axis: repeated as in the left panel—a bold horizontal base and a vertical arrowed axis.  
• Laminar Block: immediately above the wall, a thin rectangular block extends up to a modest height, representing the laminar boundary‐layer thickness δ_lam.  
• Turbulent Block: to the right of the thin block, a taller, thicker rectangular block reaches a greater height δ_turb, indicating the larger boundary‐layer thickness typical of turbulent flow under the same conditions.  
• No Curve Details: this panel abstracts the complex velocity profiles into simple layer‐thickness indicators, emphasizing that turbulence tends to increase the overall thickness of the region where velocity transitions from zero at the wall to the free‐stream value.

Caption and Context

The image is a schematic, black-and-white line drawing labeled “Figure 2.4: Roughness measure z₀.” It depicts two interrelated elements of the atmospheric boundary layer over a heterogeneous, vegetated surface:

1. Velocity Profile (left side)  
   - A vertical axis marked “z” represents height above ground.  
   - A curved profile line, bowed outward to the right, illustrates the mean horizontal wind speed U(z) increasing with height.  
   - Along that curve are small horizontal arrows pointing rightward; their length grows gradually from near zero at the surface up to a maximum at the top of the plotted region.  
   - Next to the curve, the label “U(z)” appears at the upper end of one of these arrows.  
   - Beneath the drawing, just above the ground line, an arrowed bracket indicates the roughness length z₀ – the vertical offset used in the modified logarithmic law.

2. Rough Ground and Recirculation (right side)  
   - The ground plane is drawn as a wavy line with alternating peaks and troughs; the soil below is cross-hatched at a 45° angle.  
   - At the crest of some of these micro-topographic bumps stand stylized flowers, indicating surface vegetation contributing to aerodynamic roughness.  
   - Within each trough, circular—vortex-shaped arrows illustrate separated eddies or recirculation zones just above the ground. These vortices highlight how surface irregularities induce localized flow reversal and nearly constant pressure pockets.  

Contextual equation (shown above the figure, though not part of the sketch itself) reads:  
 u = (uτ / κ) · log[(z + z₀)/z₀],  
where uτ is the friction velocity and κ the von Kármán constant. By introducing z₀, the so-called roughness height, the logarithmic wind-profile law remains well-defined even extremely close to the surface (z → 0). This visual, together with the equation, emphasizes how small-scale terrain elements and vegetation modify shear-generated turbulence in the lowest atmospheric layer.

The image is a black-and-white schematic titled “Figure 2.5: Detachment of FLow.” It depicts a two-dimensional circular cylinder immersed in a uniform flow entering from the left. The key elements and annotations are as follows:

1. Cylinder and Axes  
   • A large circle centered on the page represents the cross section of a cylinder.  
   • Two orthogonal straight lines intersect at the circle’s center: one horizontal (the free-stream flow direction) and one vertical. These serve as reference axes.

2. Incoming Free-stream Flow  
   • To the left of the cylinder, three parallel horizontal streamlines (thin lines with arrowheads) approach the cylinder from the left edge of the drawing.  
   • The middle streamline carries a small right-pointing arrow indicating the direction of the uniform upstream flow field.

3. Streamline Deflection Around the Cylinder  
   • As the flow nears the cylinder’s leading face, the three main streamlines diverge smoothly around the obstacle: the top and bottom lines curve upward and downward, respectively, hugging the cylinder contour.  
   • These curved lines skirt the cylinder’s surface, illustrating how the boundary layer wraps around the front half of the cylinder.

4. Separation Zone with Recirculation  
   • On the right (downstream) side of the cylinder, several short, stacked, slightly tilted line segments are drawn immediately adjacent to the cylinder’s surface above the horizontal axis. These indicate a region of swirling or recirculating flow.  
   • The shading of these segments grows progressively denser toward the cylinder wall, symbolizing the eddy-filled, nearly constant-pressure recirculation bubble that forms just after flow detachment.

5. Separation Point Annotation  
   • A straight slanted arrow originates from the recirculating region and points to a specific location on the cylinder’s upper surface a little behind its vertical midline.  
   • Near this arrow’s tip, the label “Separation Point” identifies the angular position where the boundary‐layer flow no longer adheres to the surface and begins to roll up into the wake.

6. Downstream Streamline Reattachment  
   • Beyond the recirculation zone, a single curved streamline is sketched rejoining the outer flow. This line, farther from the cylinder surface, illustrates the eventual recovery of flow direction in the wake.

7. Overall Flow Behavior  
   • The figure visually summarizes how an initially attached boundary layer around a bluff body (cylinder) will, under adverse pressure‐gradient conditions, separate at a distinct point.  
   • It captures the classic detachment phenomenon that gives rise to a low‐pressure recirculation bubble on the downstream side, as occurs within the lowest layer of the atmospheric boundary layer when wind encounters obstacles.

8. Relation to Boundary-Layer Theory  
   • Although the drawing itself is a generic detachment diagram, in context it serves to illustrate how modified logarithmic wind profiles and turbulence models (as provided by SOFILOAD and DOLFYN) must account for the separation and constant‐pressure recirculation regions when simulating flow over objects near the ground.

By combining the smooth upstream deflection, the clearly marked separation point, and the shaded recirculation zone, the sketch conveys the fundamental process by which a turbulent boundary layer detaches and forms a wake behind a bluff body.

   d) .dge → DOLFYN  
      – DOLFYN reads the .dge file to assemble its finite‐volume mesh.

Contextual Notes (from the accompanying text)  
- DOLFYN implements a Finite Volume Method and relies on an external geometry file (.dge) exported by SOFIMSHA.  
- Two mesh variants are supported: the primary mesh (cells = original elements, solution at cell centers) and the dual mesh (Voronoi‐based, solution at nodes, resulting in polyhedral volumes).  
- In planar systems SOFIMSHA converts QUAD elements into hexahedra of thickness 1.0, assigning patch and volume‐patch numbers based on original QUAD properties.  
- Boundary conditions in DOLFYN are applied per region number, using the “primary group number” from the export step.  
- The TEDDY module prepares general solver settings and writes them out in .din format.  
- The SOFiSTiK Database (CDB) stores and manages model data; results from DOLFYN are streamed back into CDB, allowing iterative workflows with SOFIMSHA.  

Together, the flowchart and notes make clear how TEDDY, SOFIMSHA, DOLFYN, and the CDB interoperate via .din and .dge files to support preprocessing, solution, and postprocessing in a comprehensive Finite Volume analysis environment.

DOLFYN uses the Finite Volume Method with an own geometry format The geometric file (nodes, faces, volumes) with extension .dge is exported by SOFIMSHA. There are two principal variants:
 • The primary mesh uses the existing elements as cells. The solution is calculated for the centre of these cells. This is the standard procedure for the finite volume method.
 • The dual mesh is generated by a Voronoi-process based on the faces perpendicular on the element edges. The solution is then obtained for the nodes. The finite volumes are then polyhedra. This method has large benefits for the speed and precision for generated tetrahedra meshes in 3D.
 For spatial systems the BRIC-elements are taken directly. Surfaces have to be described via QUADs or structural areas.
 For planar systems SOFIMSHA will export for DOLFYN all QUAD-Elements as hexahedra with a thickenss of 1.0, the Volume-Patch number is generated from the properties of the QUAD. The edges of the QUAD become surfaces the patch numbers for those are taken from structural edges or boundary elements defined with SOFIMSHA.
 DOLFYN boundary conditions are given for a total surface or a volume only, adressed by a unique region number. When exporting the mesh the user the primary group number will be used for this region number.

The table shown is a compact but comprehensive specification of all “FLOW”-group keywords you can include in your solver’s input deck to define the physical model of your fluid simulation. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and two logical blocks: one for flow‐model activation parameters (TURB, TEMP) and one for material and thermophysical property definitions (MAT, RHO, NUE, TREF, BET, COND, CP, K).

1. TURB  
   • Purpose: selects whether and how turbulence is modeled.  
   • Valid settings (literal strings):  
      – NONE  → laminar, no turbulence model  
      – KE    → standard k–ε turbulence  
      – RNG   → RNG k–ε variant  
      – RKE   → realizable k–ε variant  
   • Unit: LIT (text literal)  
   • Default: NONE  

2. TEMP  
   • Purpose: switches temperature‐coupling on or off, and chooses the unit system.  
   • Valid settings (literal strings):  
      – NONE  → no temperature field  
      – KELV  → temperatures in Kelvin  
      – C     → temperatures in °Celsius  
      – FAHR  → temperatures in °Fahrenheit  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NONE  

3. MAT  
   • Purpose: choose a predefined fluid material or specify a material number.  
   • Examples of built-in labels: AIR (1 bar, 20 °C), H2O (1 bar, 10 °C), CO2, O2, N2, AR, KR, XE, SF6, etc.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “–” (no predefined material; user must supply property values)  

4. RHO (Density)  
   • Description: fluid density, ρ.  
   • Unit: kg/m³  
   • Default: * (required if not using MAT or if overriding MAT)  

5. NUE (Kinematic Viscosity)  
   • Description: ν, kinematic viscosity.  
   • Unit: m²/s  
   • Default: *  

6. TREF (Reference/Initial Temperature)  
   • Description: baseline temperature at which other properties are defined.  
   • Unit: ° (in the unit system selected by TEMP)  
   • Default: *  

7. BET (Volumetric Thermal Expansion Factor)  
   • Description: β, the coefficient in the Boussinesq approximation (1/°).  
   • Unit: 1/°  
   • Default: *  

8. COND (Thermal Conductivity)  
   • Description: k, conductivity.  
   • Unit: W/(K·m)  
   • Default: *  

9. CP (Specific Heat Capacity)  
   • Description: c_p, at constant pressure.  
   • Unit: J/(kg·K)  
   • Default: *  

10. K (Compressibility Modulus)  
   • Description: bulk modulus, inverse of compressibility.  
   • Unit: MPa (×10⁹ Pa)  
   • Default: *  

Notes & Cross-References  
- The “*” default means a value must be supplied if you are not inheriting from MAT.  
- TURB and TEMP are the switches that activate extended flow physics—without them set to anything other than NONE, the solver assumes simple, isothermal laminar flow.  
- If you select a MAT entry, the solver will automatically populate RHO, NUE, CP, etc., with standard values for that material; you may then override any individual property by supplying a non-default value in the corresponding row.  
- See also the related groups and keywords: WIND (for free‐stream wind conditions), CASE (for time‐stepping and solver controls), IN/OUT (boundary conditions), WALL (wall treatments), STEP (time or iteration stepping), HIST (historical data initialization), CTRL (control variables).  
- Usage pattern in your input file:  
     FLOW  
       TURB  KE  
       TEMP  C  
       MAT   AIR  
       … (optional overrides)  

This table thus serves as both the master index of all flow‐related keywords and a quick reminder of units, default behaviors, and data dependencies—ideal for automated parsing into a RAG‐based vector store.

The input table defines all of the wind‐profile parameters that a user must supply when setting up an atmospheric‐boundary‐layer (ABL) inflow in SOFiLOAD.  At its core it links each parameter’s mnemonic (“Item”) to a concise human‐readable description, the engineering unit in which it must be specified, and a suggested default value.  Taken together, these entries control how the neutral‐equilibrium wind profile is generated at model inlet faces (steady or transient via WGEN), how roughness and measurement adjustments are handled, and how turbulence scaling is applied with height.  

Below is a detailed breakdown of every row in the table:

1. LC  
   • Description: Selects the type of wind definition or load case.  
   • Permissible values:  
     – TUNN  = wind‐tunnel profile with a ceiling (closed top)  
     – ABL   = natural open‐air boundary layer (default)  
     – lc    = user‐defined load case that contains its own wind settings  
   • Unit: –/LIT (literature code)  
   • Default: ABL  

2. V  
   • Description: Reference wind‐speed magnitude to be imposed on the inlet plane.  
   • Unit: [m/sec]  
   • Default: none (user must supply)  

3. HREF  
   • Description: Height above ground at which the reference wind speed V is measured.  
   • Unit: [m] (1006 indicates standard meteorological height tag)  
   • Default: 10.0  

4. Z0  
   • Description: Surface roughness length for the computational domain’s terrain.  This parameter controls the logarithmic wind‐speed profile near ground.  
   • Unit: [m]  
   • Default: 0.30  

5. Z0M  
   • Description: “Measured” roughness length.  Used when converting a measured wind profile from a nearby location with different terrain roughness Z0M via mass‐conservation at 300 m.  
   • Unit: [m]  
   • Default: Z0 (copy local roughness by default)  

6. LSC  
   • Description: Integral length‐scale factor, controlling the size of turbulent eddies in the vertical.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.491  

7. DX, DY, DZ  
   • Description: Cartesian components of the wind‐vector direction.  Together they form a unit vector that orients the inflow.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: DX = 0.0, DY = 0.0, DZ = 0.0  (note: if you want purely x‐directed flow, set DX = 1.0, DY = 0, DZ = 0)  

8. HG  
   • Description: Terrain elevation or “height of ground” used to shift the wind profile vertically in domains with nonzero base elevation.  
   • Unit: [m] (1006 tag)  
   • Default: none (needs user input if terrain not at z = 0)  

9. C1, C2  
   • Description: Dimensionless scaling factors for the two‐layer turbulence‐gradient model (see equations 3.2 and 3.3).  C1 typically adjusts the low‐altitude decay, while C2 fine‐tunes the outer layer.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: C1 = 0.0, C2 = 1.0  

10. HMAX  
    • Description: Maximum height up to which the logarithmic wind profile is enforced.  Above this “top‐cell” the flow is usually held constant or linked to upper‐boundary conditions.  
    • Unit: [m] (1006 tag)  
    • Default: none (determined by mesh height or user)  

Additional contextual notes:  
• When LC = ABL, the code constructs a neutral (zero‐buoyancy) atmospheric boundary layer using the standard log‐law (u(z) ≈ (u*/κ) ln((z+z0)/z0)) and the two turbulence‐scaling equations cited from Yang et al. (2009).  
• For transient wind loading, the user invokes WGEN and assigns WIND_INFL to a single group; the same table parameters then seed the spectral turbulence generator.  
• If field measurements come from a station over different terrain, Z0M lets you normalize that data back to your site’s Z0 by matching wind speeds at a reference “meso‐height” of 300 m.  

By capturing every variable, unit and default, this table acts as the single source of truth when storing and retrieving wind‐profile definitions from a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store or any engineering database.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the input table, organized by logical groups. This explanation is suitable for indexing in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store and highlights each item’s purpose, units, defaults, and how it ties into the broader workflow (FLOW, WIND, CASE, IN, OUT, INOU, WALL, STEP, HIST, CTRL).

1. Load-Case Definitions  
   • LC (Load case for results)  
     – Role: Specifies which result set to read or write.  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: 1  
   • PLC (Primary load case)  
     – Role: Establishes the baseline case from which other initial conditions may inherit values (e.g. atmospheric boundary-layer profiles).  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: none (must be provided or implied)  
   • LCD (Load case increment for differences)  
     – Role: When set, additional result cases are automatically generated. Each new case number = original LC + LCD, containing the difference between current velocities and those in PLC.  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: none  

2. Initial-Condition Variables  
   Any of these may be:  
     • Defined via PLC (inherit) or through an ABL profile,  
     • Overwritten per element by a constant numeric value or by a coordinate-dependent formula string (using variables #X, #Y, #Z).  
   • U, V, W (Initial velocity components)  
     – Description: Velocity in X, Y, Z directions.  
     – Unit: m/sec  
     – Default: unset  
   • DEN (Density)  
     – Description: Initial mass density.  
     – Unit: kg/m³  
     – Default: unset  
   • K (Turbulent energy or intensity)  
     – Description: If entered as a percentage (e.g. “2[%]”), it is treated as turbulence intensity; otherwise as specific turbulent energy.  
     – Unit: m²/sec²  
     – Default: unset  
   • EPS (Dissipation rate or length scale)  
     – Description: Can be expressed as a dissipation rate (m³/sec²) or, alternately, as a length scale (e.g. “12.4[m]”).  
     – Unit: m³/sec²  
     – Default: unset  
   • TEMP (Initial temperature)  
     – Unit: degrees (°) – scale depends on convention (Celsius, Kelvin)  
     – Default: unset  
   • P (Initial static pressure)  
     – Unit: bar  
     – Default: unset  

3. Pressure-Reference Settings  
   To define a zero‐pressure datum internally, choose one of:  
   • PREF (Reference nodal point)  
     – Role: Node ID used as zero‐pressure reference.  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: * (required if no explicit coordinates given)  
   • PRFX, PRFY, PRFZ (Explicit coordinates)  
     – Role: Use physical coordinates to mark the zero‐pressure point, bypassing node lookup.  
     – Unit: meters [m] (system length unit)  
     – Default: * (at least one method must be defined)  

4. Miscellaneous  
   • TITL (Result case designation)  
     – Description: A free-form title (up to 32 characters) used to label the result set.  
     – Data type: Lit32 (32-character literal)  
     – Default: none  

Usage Notes and Context  
– Every variable may be inherited from PLC or fully customized per element.  
– Coordinate placeholders (#X, #Y, #Z) allow field initialization via spatially varying formulas.  
– Defining LCD automates creation of “delta” cases, streamlining post-processing of velocity changes.  
– Pressure-reference entries ensure internal consistency when absolute pressures are of interest in post-processing.  
– This table is called in the CASE section of the input deck, often following the INOU definitions and preceding solver STEP instructions.

This table defines the set of inlet‐boundary parameters (or “items”) that a CFD control file can accept when prescribing boundary conditions at an inlet face.  Each row corresponds to one “Item” code, its semantic role under “Description,” the physical “Unit” in which it must be supplied, and the “Default” value the solver will assume if the item is omitted.  In practice, these entries may be inherited from a pre‐defined load case in the database (LC), or overwritten by explicit numeric values or even by spatial/time‐dependent formula strings that reference the coordinate symbols #X, #Y, #Z and/or time #T.  

1. NO  
   • Description: Region number of the boundary.  This integer labels which inlet region is being defined when multiple inlets exist.  
   • Unit: none (solver‐internal index)  
   • Default: 1  

2. LC  
   • Description: Load case in the database.  Instead of specifying individual quantities, the user can refer to a named load‐case record that carries preconfigured inlet data.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: “–” (no load case selected by default)  

3. TYP  
   • Description: Type of boundary condition (“Type der Randbedingung” in German).  Typical values include IN, OUT, WALL, STEP, HIST, etc., controlling how the solver treats the face.  
   • Unit: enumeration (not a physical unit; often shown as LIT in documentation)  
   • Default: IN  

4. U, V, W  
   • Descriptions: Velocity components of the incoming fluid in the global X, Y, and Z directions, respectively.  These define the vector inlet velocity field.  
   • Unit: meters per second [m/sec]  
   • Defaults: none (must be provided or inherited)  

5. DEN  
   • Description: Density of the incoming fluid.  If constant density is assumed, this single value applies everywhere on the inlet.  
   • Unit: kilograms per cubic meter [kg/m³]  
   • Default: none  

6. K  
   • Description: Turbulent energy or, alternatively, turbulence intensity specification.  When set as a single number, it may represent kinematic turbulent energy (½ u′²) or be derived from a percent intensity.  
   • Unit: square meters per second squared [m²/sec²]  
   • Default: none  

7. EPS  
   • Description: Turbulence dissipation rate ε, or—if the user prefers—the integral length scale of turbulence.  The solver interprets this entry according to downstream turbulence‐model settings.  
   • Unit: cubic meters per second squared [m³/sec²]  
   • Default: none  

8. TEMP  
   • Description: Temperature of the incoming fluid.  Defines the thermal inlet condition if energy equations are active.  
   • Unit: degrees (absolute or relative, depending on the solver convention) [°]  
   • Default: none  

Contextual notes:  
- Any of U, V, W, DEN, K, EPS, TEMP can be assigned by a simple numeric literal (e.g., `U = 10.0`) or by a formula string such as  
    IN 1 U ’=0.30*(1.-((#Y-0.005)/0.205)**2)’  
  which builds a parabolic profile in Y.  
- Similarly, K may be computed from a specified turbulence intensity (e.g., 2 %) and EPS from an integral length scale (e.g., 12.4 m) if those options are enabled.  
- Omitted items default to “–” except NO (defaults to region 1) and TYP (defaults to IN), which ensures there is always at least one inlet region defined.

The table shown is a concise specification for the “OUT” (outlet) boundary-condition block in a solver’s input deck. It defines exactly two parameters—NO and F—each occupying a single row. The four columns (Item, Description, Unit, Default) capture the key metadata you’d need to store in a vectorized index for fast lookup, semantic search, or prompt-based assembly of input files. Below is a breakdown of its structure and semantics, together with notes on how it relates to the broader set of boundary-condition keywords (FLOW, WIND, CASE, IN, OUT, INOU, WALL, STEP, HIST, CTRL).

1. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – A short, all-caps token that uniquely identifies the input field.  
     – In this table, the two valid tokens are “NO” and “F.”  
     – Acts as the primary key when parsing or generating the corresponding line in the configuration file.  

   • Description  
     – A human-readable explanation of what the field controls.  
     – Used in user documentation, GUI tooltips, or auto-generated schema validators.  

   • Unit  
     – The physical unit of the parameter, if applicable.  
     – Here both entries have “—,” indicating that no dimensional unit applies.  

   • Default  
     – The value assigned if the user does not explicitly override it.  
     – Serves as a fallback during input validation or when constructing a minimal input deck.  

2. Row-by-Row Semantics  
   • NO  
     – Description: “Region number of the boundary”  
     – Type: Integer index  
     – Domain: Positive integers (1, 2, 3, …) corresponding to region IDs defined elsewhere  
     – Default: 1  
     – Role: Selects which mesh region or boundary patch is treated as the outlet.  

   • F  
     – Description: “Partial factor of outlet”  
     – Type: Floating-point scalar  
     – Domain: Typically in [0.0, 1.0] or higher depending on solver support (values >1 can amplify outflow)  
     – Default: 1.0  
     – Role: Scales or modulates the mass (or volume) flux through the outlet boundary. A value of 1.0 applies the full computed flux, whereas 0.5 would pass half of it, etc.  

3. Usage Patterns & Cross-References  
   – In a complete input deck you’ll see a block headed by “OUT” followed by lines like  
        NO    1  
        F     1.0  
     or with customized values for multiple outlets.  
   – See also:  
     • IN   – for inlet boundary specifications (e.g. region number of the inlet, inlet profile)  
     • WALL – for solid walls (e.g. no-slip region ID, roughness)

The table defines the set of input parameters required to prescribe a pressure‐based inflow/outflow (INOU) boundary condition in a CFD solver. Unlike a pure IN (velocity‐specified) boundary, here the pressure P is imposed and the resulting velocity field (inward or outward) arises from the local pressure gradient. For inflow regions, additional properties—density, turbulent quantities, and temperature—must be specified so that the solver can construct a physically consistent incoming state. Variables may be set to fixed numeric values or to spatial/temporal formulae based on coordinates (#X, #Y, #Z) and time (#T). Turbulence can be defined either via turbulent energy K and dissipation rate EPS or, alternately, through turbulence intensity and integral length scale.

Column-by-column overview  
• Item: mnemonic code for each input field.  
• Description: meaning of the field.  
• Unit: physical units expected by the solver.  
• Default: value used if none is provided.

Row-by-row details  
1. NO  
   – Description: Region number identifying which boundary patch this condition applies to.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: 1.

2. LC  
   – Description: Load case reference from the solver’s database. Allows reuse of preconfigured profiles.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “–” (no load case; user must supply values manually).

3. TYPE  
   – Description: Type of boundary condition. In this context, “IN” designates a pressure‐driven inflow/outflow patch.  
   – Unit: literal (LIT).  
   – Default: “IN”.

4. P  
   – Description: Static pressure value on the boundary. Positive gradients drive outflow; negative gradients cause inflow.  
   – Unit: bar.  
   – Default: none (must be specified or inherited from a load case).

5. DEN  
   – Description: Density of the incoming fluid, used only if the boundary acts as an inflow.  
   – Unit: kg/m³.  
   – Default: none.

6. K  
   – Description: Turbulent kinetic energy per unit mass (or, if desired, turbulence intensity can be converted internally to K).  
   – Unit: m²/s².  
   – Default: none.

7. EPS  
   – Description: Dissipation rate of turbulence (alternatively, an integral length scale may be supplied, from which EPS is derived).  
   – Unit: m³/s².  
   – Default: none.

8. TEMP  
   – Description: Temperature of the incoming fluid, required when mass enters the domain.  
   – Unit: degrees (°).  
   – Default: none.

– Inlet conditions can be driven by a predefined atmospheric boundary‐layer profile or by custom expressions.  
– Any of the fluid properties (DEN, K, EPS, TEMP) may be overridden individually.

The table defines the input parameters for a “WALL” boundary region in a computational-fluid-dynamics (CFD) case.  Any boundary not explicitly tagged as IN (inlet) or OUT (outlet) defaults to WALL.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown, with units, defaults and physical meaning.  See also related keywords: FLOW, WIND, CASE, IN, OUT, INOU, STEP, HIST, CTRL.

1. NO  
   • Description: Index or region number of this wall boundary.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless integer)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Notes: Used to identify multiple wall patches when setting up boundary conditions.

2. Z0  (Roughness of the Wall)  
   • Description: Specifies how the wall interacts with turbulence and the near-wall velocity profile.  
     – x.xx: explicit roughness height zo in meters, activating a logarithmic wall law (valid for y+ > 1.0).  
     – SLIP: non-adherent, hydraulically smooth surface; enforces zero normal velocity while leaving tangential velocity unconstrained, and drives turbulence parameters k, ε to zero.  
     – NOSL: adherent, hydraulically smooth wall (no slip, no-adherence of turbulence).  
     – SYMP: natural (symmetry) boundary; fluid is forced parallel to the wall with no other interaction.  
   • Unit: m (for numerical zo only)  
   • Default: NOSL  
   • Context: The explicit roughness model may refer to equivalent roughness from EC 1 part 2-4 (e.g. cast iron ≈0.2 m/30 ≈0.0067 m).  SLIP and NOSL offer simpler, idealized treatments; SYMP imposes a free-slip, zero-normal-flux condition.

3. U, V, W  (Velocity Components)  
   • Description: Prescribed wall-normal and tangential velocities:  
     – U: X-direction  
     – V: Y-direction  
     – W: Z-direction  
   • Unit: m/sec  
   • Default: –  (not prescribed unless needed, implying zero normal velocity with SLIP/NOSL or free-slip under SYMP)

4. TEMP  (Wall Temperature)  
   • Description: Static temperature at the wall surface.  
   • Unit: degrees (°)  
   • Default: * (asterisk indicates inherited or case-wide default if not specified)

5. R  (Linear Heat Conduction Resistance)  
   • Description: Represents heat conduction through a solid wall layer as a linear thermal resistance.  Used in series with convective heat transfer to the fluid.  
   • Unit: W / °C / m²  (interpreted as thermal resistance per unit area)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes: If neither R nor HFLX is provided, the wall is treated as adiabatic (no heat exchange).

6. RADI  (Emissivity for Radiation Boundary)  
   • Description: Surface emission coefficient for thermal radiation.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless, 0–1)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes: Governs radiative heat flux; 0=black body absorption/emission disabled.

7. HFLX  (Prescribed Heat Flux)  
   • Description: Imposed net heat flux at the wall.  Positive values correspond to heat input into the fluid domain.  
   • Unit: W/m²  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes: Overrides convective exchange if specified; combined with R and radiative effects for total wall energy balance.

How It All Fits Together  
– Velocity BC: SLIP or NOSL enforce different tangential constraints; explicit Z0 triggers a log-law wall treatment if y+ > 1.  SYMP acts as a zero-normal gradient symmetry plane.  
– Thermal BC:  
   1. Convection to fluid (linked to turbulence model)  
   2. Conduction through wall (via R)  
   3. Radiation (via RADI)  
   4. Direct flux specification (via HFLX)  
If R and HFLX are omitted, the wall defaults to adiabatic. This table encapsulates all necessary inputs to fully define both hydrodynamic and thermal behavior at wall boundaries in a CFD simulation.

The provided table is a catalogue of typical equivalent sand-grain roughness values (k) expressed in millimetres for a variety of engineering surfaces. These values serve as reference inputs for defining the “roughness” boundary condition in CFD simulations (when using a logarithmic wall‐law approach), provided the nondimensional wall‐distance y+ exceeds unity.  When an explicit k is specified, the solver enforces a no‐slip velocity condition at the wall while allowing turbulence quantities to adjust naturally according to the chosen wall‐law.  If a roughness height k is not given, many codes will treat the wall as hydraulically smooth (SLIP) or even adiabatic with no heat flux if no thermal resistance is defined.

Summary of Surfaces and Their Roughness Values:
  • Very Smooth Finishes (k on the order of 10⁻³ mm)
    – Glass: 0.0015 mm  
    – Polished metal: 0.002 mm  
    – Smooth painting: 0.006 mm  

  • Lightly Textured or Coated Surfaces (k on the order of 10⁻² mm)
    – Spray painting: 0.02 mm  
    – Blasted steel: 0.05 mm  

  • Common Structural Metals (k on the order of 10⁻¹ mm)
    – Cast iron: 0.20 mm  
    – Galvanised steel: 0.20 mm  

  • Concrete and Masonry (k from 10⁻¹ mm up to single‐digit mm)
    – Spinning (trowelled) concrete: 0.20 mm  
    – Cast-in-situ concrete: 1.0 mm  
    – Rust (oxidised steel surfaces): 2.0 mm  
    – Masonry (brick or blockwork faces): 3.0 mm  

Key points for application:
 1.  The explicit roughness value k replaces the default smooth‐wall assumption (SYMP or SLIP) and forces the turbulence model to adjust near‐wall eddy viscosity and turbulent kinetic energy dissipation accordingly.  
 2.  When using the EC 1 part 2–4 guideline, one may estimate the equivalent roughness length zo by dividing k by approximately 30 (zo ≈ k/30), facilitating cross‐validation with wind-engineering standards.  
 3.  In the absence of any user‐defined wall‐roughness (R) or imposed wall heat‐flux (HFLX), the wall is assumed adiabatic.  If wall thermal resistance is relevant, the solver will add a linear conduction resistance term based on wall material thickness and conductivity.

The table presented here defines the key control parameters for any transient (time-dependent) or iterative (steady-state) analysis in the solver.  Each row represents one input keyword, its role in defining time/iteration behaviour, the units expected, and the built-in default if you omit it.  Taken together, they allow you to control how the solver marches through time or iterates to convergence.

1. N  – Number of time/iteration steps  
   • Description: Specifies either the total count of time increments in a transient run or, if no transient time is given, the maximum number of nonlinear iteration loops in a steady-state solve.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: 500  

   Usage notes:  
     – If you intend a time-accurate transient simulation, set N ≥1 to fix exactly that many time steps.  
     – If you omit the total analysis time (T), the solver assumes a steady-state problem and uses N as the iteration cap.

2. T  – Time value of first step or total analysis time  
   • Description: When N ≥1, T is taken as the duration of the first time step (from which subsequent steps can grow).  When N <1, T defines the full duration of the transient run and N is treated as a fraction of T for the first step.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: none (must be specified for transient analysis)

   Usage notes:  
     – N <1 (e.g. N=0.001) yields an initial step of N×T (one-thousandth of the total run time), then remains constant unless progression is applied.  
     – If you do not define T at all, the solver switches to steady-state mode.

3. TFAK  – Factor for time-step progression  
   • Description: Multiplicative growth factor between successive time steps in a geometric progression.  If you choose to let your time-step size grow, each new step Δtₙ₊₁ = Δtₙ × TFAK.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: none

   Usage notes:  
     – Use with caution: large values of TFAK combined with large initial Δt can cause overly large time-steps.  
     – Always double-check the resulting time-step sequence with a calculator or small test run.

4. DTM  – Maximum time-step size limit  
   • Description: Caps each time increment so it never exceeds this value, even if TFAK would produce a larger step.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: 1

   Usage notes:  
     – Helps maintain stability and resolution in rapidly changing flows by preventing runaway time-step growth.

5. INT  – Interval for saving a result case  
   • Description: Number of seconds (or fraction thereof) between write-outs of solution files.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: none

   Usage notes:  
     – If left blank, the solver may only write at the end of the run (or at every step if forced by other settings).

6. TOL  – Tolerance for iterations  
   • Description: Convergence criterion for inner nonlinear/linear solver loops.  Iterations continue until the residual norm drops below TOL.  
   • Unit: dimensionless  
   • Default: 1e-4

   Usage notes:  
     – Tight tolerances slow each time step but improve accuracy.  Looser tolerances speed progression but risk poor physical fidelity.

7. TORD  – Time-integration scheme  
   • Description: Chooses the algorithmic order or blend between first-order implicit Euler and second-order quadratic schemes.  
     – LINE  = standard first-order implicit Euler  
     – QUAD  = true second-order quadratic accurate in time  
     – value = any number between 0.0 and 1.0 to blend LINE and QUAD schemes proportionally  
   • Unit: dimensionless / flag “LIT”  
   • Default: LINE

   Usage notes:  
     – LINE is more robust and unconditionally stable but more diffusive.  
     – QUAD gives higher temporal accuracy but can require smaller Δt (or tighter TOL) to remain stable.  
     – A blending factor (e.g. 0.5) can offer a compromise between stability and accuracy.

The table presented defines the key parameters controlling how DOLFYN (or a similar CFD kernel) assembles and solves the discrete equations for various flow and scalar fields.  Each row (“Item”) names a parameter; the “Description” column explains its purpose and allowable codes; “Unit” indicates the expected data type (LIT for literal strings, “–” for dimensionless numbers); and “Default” gives the built-in value applied if the user does not override it.  Below is a detailed walk-through of every table entry, with context drawn from the accompanying documentation snippet.

1. VAR (Name of Variable)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “!” (i.e. must be specified)  
   • Purpose: Selects which equation(s) the following solver parameters apply to.  Valid literals include:  
     – ALL: all variables  
     – U, V, W: individual velocity components  
     – UVW: the full velocity vector system  
     – P: pressure  
     – K: turbulent kinetic energy  
     – EPS: turbulent dissipation rate  
     – KEPS: shorthand for both K and EPS (all turbulent-parameter equations)  
     – T: temperature equation  
     – SCAL: any other passive scalar  
   • Notes:  No differencing scheme exists for pressure (P); the user must couple P with a solver (WITH) that handles an algebraic pressure correction.

2. DIFF (Differencing Scheme)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (inherits from a parent block if unspecified)  
   • Purpose: Chooses the spatial discretization scheme for convective and diffusive terms.  Options are:  
     – OFF: skip solving this equation  
     – ON: invoke the default internal solver  
     – UD: Upwind Differencing (first-order, highly diffusive)  
     – CD: Central Differencing (second- or third-order, CD2/CD3)  
     – LUX: Linear Upwind with limiters (e.g. LUD, MIN)—balances stability and accuracy  
     – GAM: Jasak’s blending of UD and CD1 (essentially a 0.5–0.75 hybrid)  
   • Context:  LUX is the default for velocity and turbulent scalars on hexahedral meshes; GAM is default for temperature.

3. BLEN (Blending Factor)  
   • Unit: “–” (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 1.0  
   • Purpose: If DIFF=GAM, this factor weights UD vs. CD1.  A value of 1.0 means pure UD; lower values introduce more CD.

4. SLOP (Slope Limiter Functionality)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: VNF  
   • Purpose: When using LUX or other higher-order schemes, a limiter can be applied to suppress non-physical oscillations.  Options are:  
     – VNF: Venkatakrishnan limiter at faces  
     – P1F: Polynomial limiter adapted at face centers

5. WITH (Solver for Variable)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (inherit)  
   • Purpose: Determines which linear algebraic solver or preconditioner to use for the chosen equation.  Examples:  
     – MKL: Intel MKL’s GMRES solver (pressure only)  
     – (Other solvers such as BiCG, PISO, SIMPLE may be available depending on the code build.)  
   • Parallelism: To run in parallel, the user can append a directive like “DOLF use cores 4.”

6. RELA (Relaxation Factor)  
   • Unit: “–” (dimensionless)  
   • Default: “*”  
   • Purpose: Under-relaxes the update to the solution in each outer iteration.  Typical values range from 0.3 to 1.0.  
   • Notes:  Stronger under-relaxation (e.g. 0.3–0.5) can enhance stability, especially on skewed or tetrahedral meshes.

Additional Context from Documentation  
• Initialization phase (via DOLF INIT STEPS nn) temporarily forces all WALL boundaries to symmetric (“SYMP”) and uses UD differencing for a few iterations to build a smooth initial field.  
• A suggested startup strategy is to run a short transient with UD (blending 0.8–1.0) plus a slope limiter (VNF) before switching to higher-order schemes (LUX or GAM) for the steady solve.

The table in question defines how arbitrary DOLFYN input lines (“DOLF” commands) are captured and stored within the CADINP→DOLF interface. In short, any parameter or command that cannot be expressed through the standard CADINP keywords (FLOW, WIND, CASE, IN, OUT, WALL, STEP, HIST, CTRL, etc.) must be written into a “DOLF” block; this table governs the format of each entry in that block.

1. Table Purpose  
   •  Enables users to inject free-form DOLFYN directives at the end of every generated CADINP deck.  
   •  Provides a minimal metadata schema so that each custom line can be passed verbatim (“literal”) to the DOLFYN solver.  
   •  Ensures that CADINP’s parser treats these lines as opaque strings rather than attempting to interpret or validate them.

2. Column-by-Column Breakdown  
   1) Item  
     – Acts as a user-defined tag or identifier for each DOLF line.  
     – Typically left blank or set to a short mnemonic if one wants to refer back to it in higher-level scripts.  
     – Not strictly required by the solver, but can aid in organizing multiple DOLF entries.  
   2) Description  
     – Contains the full text of the DOLFYN command or parameter set.  
     – Before the CADINP file is passed to the DOLFYN executable, any placeholders or variables are replaced with their actual numeric or string values.  
     – Examples:  
         • “INIT STEP 0” (skips laminar initial iterations)  
         • “restart” (restart from previous solution)  
         • “restart initial” (use restart as the initial guess)  
     – Any legal DOLFYN directive may be placed here; one simply types the exact command as if editing the .din file by hand.  
   3) Unit  
     – Always set to “Lit” (short for “literal”).  
     – Indicates that the Description field is a free-form string, not a numeric value with physical units.  
     – CADINP’s preprocessor will not attempt unit conversion or validation on these entries.  
   4) Default  
     – Left blank in the standard template, signaling that no default DOLF command is assumed.  
     – If required, a site-wide or project-wide default could be supplied here (e.g. “INIT STEP 0”), but typically every entry is user-supplied.  

3. How It Fits Into the Workflow  
   – In the CADINP deck you would see a block labeled “DOLF” at the end of your keyword summary.  
   – For each DOLF line you wish to include you append one row following this table schema.  
   – When CADINP writes out the final .din file for DOLFYN, it concatenates all Description fields verbatim (in the same order) ahead of or after the main body.  
   – To run DOLFYN directly on that .din file, you might call:  
         dolfyn mycase.din –i  
     Where “–i” tells DOLFYN to immediately enter interactive/testing mode.  

4. Special Hints & Common Patterns  
   – “DOLF INIT STEP 0” → forces DOLFYN to skip any automatic laminar‐flow initial iterations.  
   – “DOLF restart”  → instructs DOLFYN to pull in a previously saved solution.  
   – “DOLF restart initial” → similar to the above but uses the restart dataset as the starting guess for the nonlinear solver.  
   – More advanced sequences (multi‐step restarts, parameter sweeps, custom solver controls) are documented in the Dolfyn Input Guide—these all live in this same table.  

In practice, you will typically define one or more “DOLF” entries whenever the stock CADINP keywords cannot express a new boundary condition, solver control parameter, or post-processing switch exposed by the latest DOLFYN releases. By centralizing them in this single “DOLF” table, downstream automation and RAG‐style retrieval can locate and manipulate custom solver directives without parsing the geometry or physics sections directly.

The table presents a systematic convergence study for the unsteady two-dimensional cylinder flow at Reynolds number Re = 100. It collates five computational runs at three mesh‐refinement “levels,” each differing by the total number of control volumes and the number of time‐steps over which the vortex shedding process was sampled. A final “reference” line gives target values taken from the DFG Benchmark data set.

1. Columns and meaning  
   • Level: an integer mesh‐refinement index (2, 3 or 4). Higher levels correspond to progressively finer spatial resolutions.  
   • Volumes: the number of finite‐volume cells used in the domain. Level 2 uses only 552 cells, level 3 uses 2 208 cells, and level 4 uses 8 832 cells.  
   • Time-steps: the number of discrete time‐levels over which the lift and drag signals were recorded—essentially the length and temporal resolution of the shedding cycle.  
   • Cd (drag coefficient): mean drag on the cylinder, averaged over the sampled time history.  
   • Cl (lift coefficient amplitude): half the peak-to-peak oscillation of lift, a direct measure of vortex‐shedding strength.  
   • St (Strouhal number): the dimensionless shedding frequency fD/U, where D is cylinder diameter and U the mean inflow speed. A dash (“–”) indicates that no clear periodic shedding was captured.  
   • CPU: total computational cost on a single processing unit (in arbitrary “CPU‐time” units).

2. Row-by-row synopsis  
   • Level 2, 552 vols, 500 steps: Cd = 3.18 is within 2 % of the reference 3.23, but Cl = 0.040 is essentially zero—no sustained vortex shedding develops. Accordingly, St cannot be defined. CPU cost is minimal (24).  
   • Level 3, 2 208 vols, 500 steps: Cd rises slightly to 3.36 (+4 % error), Cl = 0.392 begins to reflect some vortex shedding, and St = 0.250 is about 17 % below the reference 0.300. CPU time increases to 174.  
   • Level 4, 8 832 vols, 1 000 steps: best approximation of the shedding process. Cd = 3.27 (–1 % error), Cl = 0.694 (still ~37 % below the reference Cl = 1.10), and St = 0.275 (–8 % error). CPU cost jumps to 1 516.  
   • Level 4, 8 832 vols, 500 steps: same spatial resolution but half the temporal sampling. Cd returns to 3.18, Cl = 0.558, St = 0.267 (–11 %), and CPU drops to 1 171. Reduced time‐history impairs both the mean force prediction and shedding amplitude.  
   • Level 4, 8 832 vols, 200 steps: coarse temporal sampling again kills the vortex‐shedding signal (Cl = 0.083, St undefined), although drag remains near 3.09. CPU is 590.  

3. Comparison to reference  
   The published benchmark values are Cd = 3.23, Cl = 1.10, and St = 0.300. Even at the finest mesh (level 4) and longest run (1 000 steps), the lift amplitude is underpredicted by ~37 % and shedding frequency by ~8 %.  

4. Key observations  
   – Spatial refinement alone (going from level 2 to level 3) is not sufficient to capture vortex shedding; temporal resolution must also be adequate.  
   – At the finest mesh, doubling the number of time-steps from 500 to 1 000 measurably improves both Cl and St but at a steep CPU‐time penalty (≈30 % more cost).  
   – Coarse time sampling on any mesh suppresses shedding altogether, illustrating the coupled importance of mesh density and time‐step count in resolving the Kármán vortex street.  

5. Contextual note  
   These runs assume a hydraulically smooth cylinder, 5 % inlet‐turbulence intensity, and turbulence length scale equal to the cylinder diameter. The table demonstrates that even with millions of unknowns available in the full DFG benchmark, moderate meshes and time‐resolutions can yield reasonable drag predictions but struggle to reproduce lift and shedding frequency accurately without careful meshing and sufficiently long transient sampling.

• Curve behavior  
  – All three curves begin at φ = 0° (the front stagnation point) at cₚ ≈ +1, indicating stagnation pressure.  
  – As φ increases from 0° toward 30°, each curve drops sharply as the flow accelerates around the cylinder shoulder.  
  – Subcritical (dashed):  
    • Drops moderately to cₚ ≈ –0.5 by φ ≈ 30°.  
    • Declines more slowly beyond 30°, crossing the zero line just before φ ≈ 60°, then flattening out above cₚ ≈ –1.0 all the way toward φ = 120°.  
    • Indicates early separation and wider wake.  
  – Supercritical (dash-dot):  
    • Falls more steeply, reaching a minimum around cₚ ≈ –2.5 at φ ≈ 60°.  
    • After this deepest trough, the curve rises gradually, crossing back above cₚ ≈ –1.0 near φ ≈ 100° and trending toward zero by φ = 120°.  
    • Reflects delayed separation and a much narrower wake (the “drag crisis” regime).  
  – Transcritical (solid):  
    • Exhibits an intermediate drop, bottoming out at cₚ ≈ –1.8 around φ ≈ 55°.  
    • Shows a secondary inflection (a small hump) around φ ≈ 85° where cₚ briefly climbs toward –1.0, then dips slightly again before slowly rising to about –0.5 at φ = 120°.  
    • Represents behaviour just beyond the critical regime, blending features of both sub- and supercritical flows.  

• Physical interpretation  
  – The graph demonstrates the “cylinder crisis” or drag-crisis phenomenon: at subcritical Reynolds numbers, early boundary-layer separation produces a relatively high drag (flatter cₚ curve, less suction). As Re increases into the supercritical range, the boundary layer remains attached much farther around the cylinder, causing a much deeper suction peak (lower minimum cₚ) and reduced drag. By transcritical Reynolds numbers, the flow transitions again, with multiple inflection points indicating intermittent separation and reattachment.  
  – Angles φ correspond to positions measured along the cylinder surface from the front stagnation point in the flow direction. Deep minima in cₚ correspond to regions of highest local velocity and lowest pressure. Variation among the three curves illustrates how surface pressure distribution—and thus drag and lift—changes dramatically across the drag-crisis Reynolds-number window.  

• Context note  
  Although the surrounding text discusses low-Re (20 and 100) CFD benchmarks for 2D cylinder flows, this figure specifically concerns high-Re experiments (10⁵–10⁷) in the so-called “critical” and “transcritical” regimes, where turbulent transition in the boundary layer produces a sudden drop in drag.

 The first difficulty is given by the selection of the inflow conditions for the wind. For the original project extended CFD studies for the terrain have been performed, for the CFD and wind tunnel we have to generalize the inflow. The wind tunnel report gave a turbulence intensity of 9-10 %. Assuming a roughness of 0.30 m and a height of the bridge deck of 200 m, we get a turbulence intensity of 9.4 %. The integral length scale is 81.0 m.
 For the service state wind shields have been added, which have been modelled in the wind tunnel with perforated plates with 50 % permeability. A perfect match of results should not be anticipated therefore.
 An other question is if one should model the wind tunnel model (scale 1:75) or the real struc- ture. In that case we used the real world dimensions, which is recommended by us in general.
 In that case a 2D-Analysis is performed. To select the analysis model properly one should take care of the parameters for some fundamental questions:
 • Distance of the section to the boundaries above and below. If one selects to small dis- tances, the blocking effect will disturb the pressures obtained considerably. It is recom- mended to block at most 4 % of the flow area, better is 1 to 2 %.
 Length of the area behind and the mesh density. If the mesh behind the section has a coarse mesh or is not long enough, vortices may not be modelled properly and the variation in time may not be obtained at all. Stationary mean values of the pressures may be obtained however in most cases with the k-ε-Turbulence model. The recommendation is to use an extension of 10 to 15 times the bridge width.
